actions: protracts the scapula, upwardly rotates it, and holds the scapula flush against the thoracic wall (preventing winging)

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Its long thoracic nerve runs an unusually long, superficial course over the ribs, making it especially vulnerable to injury (e.g. during axillary surgery); paralysis produces the classic 'winged scapula' sign, since serratus anterior is the primary muscle holding the scapula against the chest wall.
functional_compartments.source: Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

source: Gray's Anatomy for Students, 4th ed. (Drake, Vogl, Mitchell); Terminologia Anatomica (FICAT 1998); Holzbaur KR, Murray WM, Delp SL (2005) Ann Biomed Eng 33(6):829-840 -- upper-extremity muscle architecture model (fascicle length, pennation, PCSA)

ultrasound_injection_approach.transducer_placement: Transverse/oblique scan in the mid-axillary line at the level of the 4th-5th rib, the level of the original description. Two planes are targeted relative to the muscle: superficial SAPB (between latissimus dorsi/teres major and the superficial surface of serratus anterior) and deep SAPB (between serratus anterior and the ribs/intercostal muscles).
ultrasound_injection_approach.depth_layer: Superficial plane sits between latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior; deep plane sits between serratus anterior and the rib periosteum/external intercostal muscles, immediately superficial to the pleura.
ultrasound_injection_approach.identification_cues: Latissimus dorsi and serratus anterior are seen as two distinct muscle layers sliding over the rib shadows in the mid-axillary line; the long thoracic nerve can sometimes be seen running on the muscle's superficial surface.
structures_at_risk: pleura and lung, directly deep to the deep-plane injection point -- pneumothorax is the principal serious risk
long thoracic nerve, running on the superficial surface of the muscle -- can be blocked incidentally, producing transient winged scapula
thoracodorsal artery, vein and nerve, running with latissimus dorsi just superficial to the block plane
lateral cutaneous branches of the intercostal nerves (T2-T9), the actual analgesic target as they pierce the muscle
ultrasound_injection_approach.notes: The serratus anterior plane block (SAPB) is one of the most widely adopted ultrasound-guided truncal fascial plane blocks, used for analgesia after thoracic surgery, rib fractures, breast surgery and minimally invasive cardiac surgery; superficial and deep variants provide comparable analgesia in most reports, with the deep plane theoretically closer to the intercostal nerves as they exit the intercostal space.
ultrasound_injection_approach.source: Blanco R, Parras T, McDonnell JG, Prats-Galino A (2013) Anaesthesia 68(11):1107-1113, doi:10.1111/anae.12344 -- original description of the ultrasound-guided serratus plane block (PubMed); Vandenbrande J et al. (2024) Reg Anesth Pain Med 49(6):429-435, doi:10.1136/rapm-2023-104439 -- randomized trial of combined deep+superficial SAPB after minimally invasive cardiac surgery (PubMed)

trigger_points.location_description: Trigger points most often in the digitations over ribs 5-7 at/near the mid-axillary line
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: Antero-lateral chest-wall pain at mid-chest level (the exertional 'side stitch'), a projection to the lower medial border/inferior angle of the scapula, and down the medial (ulnar) arm and forearm to the palm and ring finger; may create a sense of 'can't take a deep breath' and air-hunger with pain on full inspiration -- a cardiac/pleuritic mimic.
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Painful deep inspiration, pain running/coughing, fatigue on prolonged forward reach.
trigger_points.notes: Check the ipsilateral latissimus dorsi and pectoral muscles together, since their trigger-point referral zones overlap here.
trigger_points.source: Simons, Travell & Simons Trigger Point Manual -- as cited in this atlas's uploaded shoulder muscle reference document (Donnelly JM, Fernandez-de-las-Penas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds), Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual, 3rd ed., Wolters Kluwer, 2019)

clinical.function_biomechanics: Protraction and the dominant share of scapular upward rotation (lower fibres) in the trapezius–serratus couple; holds the medial border and inferior angle applied to the thorax; posteriorly tilts the scapula in elevation (clearing the subacromial outlet); reach-and-punch accelerator and eccentric controller of retraction; with the scapula fixed it can raise the ribs as an accessory inspiratory muscle. Reduced serratus activity and the resulting loss of posterior tilt/upward rotation is a core mechanism of scapular dyskinesis and impingement; retraining staples: push-up plus, dynamic hug, wall slides.
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: Infraserratus (serratus–thorax) and supraserratus (serratus–subscapularis) bursae — the two consistent scapulothoracic bursae; adventitious bursae at the superomedial and inferior angles when irritated (snapping scapula). Adjacent structures — mutual influence: Long thoracic nerve palsy → medial winging (whole medial border lifts, worse on forward wall-push) with aching from levator/rhomboid overload; ribs and intercostals beneath (rib stress injuries in overhead athletes); scapulothoracic bursitis/crepitus in its planes; breast/axillary surgery field.

trigger_points.location: TrPs most often in the digitations of ribs 5–7 at/near the mid-axillary line; check ipsilateral latissimus and pectorals together.
trigger_points.referred_pain: Antero-lateral chest-wall pain at mid-chest level (the exertional “side stitch”), a projection to the lower medial border/inferior angle of the scapula, and down the medial (ulnar) arm and forearm to the palm and ring finger; may create a sense of “can’t take a deep breath” and air-hunger with pain on full inspiration — a cardiac/pleuritic mimic.
trigger_points.source: Donnelly JM, Fernández-de-las-Peñas C, Finnegan M, Freeman JL (eds). Travell, Simons & Simons’ Myofascial Pain and Dysfunction: The Trigger Point Manual. 3rd ed. Wolters Kluwer; 2019. Muscle chapters as named in each section.

pain_referred_into_this_muscle_from: Into the lateral chest/serratus zone: intercostal and rib pathology (fracture, costochondritis), pleuritic pain, latissimus TrP2, pectoralis major costal fibres
into the inferior-angle spot: latissimus TrP1 and lower-trapezius points.
clinical.movement_restrictions_aggravators: Painful deep inspiration, pain running/coughing, fatigue on prolonged forward reach; with palsy, loss of overhead endurance and pain from compensators.
clinical.notes: New winging + severe shoulder-girdle pain that preceded weakness → think neuralgic amyotrophy rather than compression; most long-thoracic palsies recover over 6–24 months with load management.
clinical.caveat: Trigger-point locations and referral maps derive from the Travell–Simons clinical-observational tradition, now standardised by Delphi consensus criteria [32] and supported by prevalence and hyperalgesia studies in shoulder pain [30,31]; they are expert-level evidence, not trial-level, and inter-examiner reliability of TrP palpation is moderate. Facet, ACJ and subacromial referral patterns, by contrast, come from experimental provocation in volunteers/patients [33,34,37]. Textbook anatomy is cited at section level; where major texts disagree (segmental levels), the range is given and flagged. Figures and patterns older than 12 months are anatomical/physiological constants and are not considered stale.
